newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss back rapid probe of Nazi-era banking.
newsitem.headline: Swiss back rapid probe of Nazi-era banking.

text.p: The Swiss government on Monday backed a rapid but thorough investigation into the fate of Nazi loot and Jewish riches put in secretive Swiss banks for safety before and during World War Two.
The Federal Council, or cabinet, approved a decree to create a commission of experts empowered to lift tight bank secrecy rules for an accounting of Swiss financial dealings with Nazi Germany.

It will also review how much wealth was deposited with Swiss banks and other financial companies by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution and whether Swiss law has done enough to identify the lost assets of those killed in the Holocaust.

Speaking for the cabinet, Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti said the need for a thorough historical accounting was shown by a recent bout of speculation that Switzerland could still be hoarding tonnes of Nazi gold.
"There is no doubt that these accusations have badly damaged Switzerland's image," Cotti told a news conference.
"It is therefore all the more important to investigate Switzerland's financial relations with Nazi Germany rapidly but at the same time with the necessary thoroughness and seriousness," he said.
Cotti said any legal or political consequences of the study would have to wait for its final conclusions.

The commission, which could start work next April, is separate from an international panel set up by Swiss banks and world Jewish groups last May to search for lost Holocaust accounts and help return them to their legal heirs.
The commission of six to 12 historians and financial and legal experts is expected to get final approval from parliament in the current autumn session and will have five years to complete its report.
A British Foreign Office report last week increased pressure on Swiss leaders to counter speculation that Nazi gold was still hidden in the neutral country's central bank.

The report, although based on documents made public long ago and known by historians, revived allegations that the Swiss kept nearly nine-tenths of gold bought from Hitler's Germany rather than hand it over to the Allies after World war Two.

Swiss National Bank (SNB) president Hans Meyer, replying to those allegations at the same news conference with Cotti, noted the SNB had acknowledged in 1985 that it had been too trusting of Germany in buying 1.2 billion Swiss francs (about $300 million at 1946 exchange rates) worth of gold between 1938 and 1945.
Asked whether the SNB could still have gold in its reserves that was bought from Hitler's Reichsbank, he said: "I cannot answer that with a yes or a no."

But Meyer said all legal obligations for the return of Nazi gold had been settled by a 1946 agreement with the Allied powers to pay them a settlement of 250 million Swiss francs (about $60 million at the time).
The settlement was compensation for gold bought from Hitler's Reichsbank during the war despite Allied warnings that much of it was stolen from central banks of countries occupied by Germany.
"This was not one of the best pages in the history of the national bank and I do not hesitate to say that we regret it," Meyer said.

Swiss parliamentarians began drafting the bill for a historical commission at the cabinet's request in May, after world Jewish groups wrung an agreement from Swiss banks to repeat a 1960s search for lost Holocaust accounts.
